explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is an open-source, CLI-based video & media downloader written in Go.  
   - It supports dozens of websites by registering a per-site “extractor” plug-in that knows how to parse URLs, call out to the site APIs or scrape pages, and emit downloadable media streams.

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top-level entry points:
     • main.go  
     • app/app.go & app/register.go (command registration & dispatch)  
   - Core sub-systems:
     • parser/ (detect site from URL, choose extractor)  
     • extractors/ (subdirectories per site, each implement the same interface)  
     • downloader/ (download logic, multi-threading, retry, resume)  
     • request/ (HTTP client, cookie & proxy handling)  
     • utils/ (pool, ffmpeg wrapper, common helpers)  
     • config/ (global configuration values)  
   - Other:
     • script/ (CI template generator)  
     • .github/workflows/ (CI/CD build, test, release)  
     • Cask.toml, goreleaser.yml (packaging)  

3. Examine the README for additional insights
   - Describes usage of CLI flags  
   - Mentions FFmpeg as an external dependency for merging fragments  
   - Shows JSON-output mode (“-j”) for reusing extracted data  
   - Details supported sites (each backed by one extractor plug-in)

4. Designing the system diagram
   a. Main components
     • User (CLI invocation)  
     • CLI core (app, register)  
     • URL Parser (parser/)  
     • Extractor Factory (registry of extractors)  
     • Extractor Plug-ins (extractors/<site>/…)  
     • HTTP Request Layer (request/)  
     • Download Engine (downloader/)  
     • Utility Layer (utils/, config/)  
     • External Tools (FFmpeg, Aria2)  
     • File System (output directory)  
     • CI/CD Pipeline (GitHub Actions, goreleaser)  

   b. Relationships & data flow
     1. User runs `lux [options] <URL>` →  
     2. CLI core (app) parses flags & hands URLs to URL Parser →  
     3. Parser identifies site & calls Extractor Factory →  
     4. Factory returns the correct Extractor Plug-in →  
     5. Extractor uses HTTP Request Layer to fetch page/API data →  
     6. Extractor parses response and emits one or more Stream descriptors →  
     7. Depending on flags (`-i`, `-j` vs download), either:
        • Print info / JSON  
        • Or invoke Download Engine:
             – Download Engine uses a Pool (utils/pool) of worker goroutines  
             – Each worker uses HTTP Request Layer to fetch media chunks  
             – After download, if multiple fragments, calls FFmpeg wrapper (utils/ffmpeg) to merge  
     8. Files are saved to disk (File System)  
     9. For packaging & releases, CI/CD pipeline auto-builds, tests, and publishes via goreleaser  

   c. Architectural patterns & principles
     • Plug-in / Factory Pattern: extractors are self-contained but share an interface  
     • Dependency Injection: request module injected into extractors and downloader  
     • Concurrency: worker pool for parallel downloads, controlled via utils/pool  
     • Single binary, modular packages: separate concerns by package  

   d. Key technologies & libraries
     • Go standard library (net/http, flag, io)  
     • goroutines & channels (utils/pool)  
     • FFmpeg (external CLI for fragment merging)  
     • Aria2 RPC (optional)  
     • goreleaser & Homebrew/Cask for packaging  
     • GitHub Actions for CI  

5. Guidelines specific to an open-source CLI tool
   - Emphasize the “plug-in” boundary: show each extractor folder as a module block with a common interface to the parser/factory.  
   - Show how network calls flow through the HTTP Request Layer and how cookies/proxies are injected.  
   - Highlight the download pipeline (worker pool → per-stream download → optional FFmpeg merge).  
   - Illustrate the extensibility: adding a new extractor is simply implementing the interface, then registering it in app/register.go.

6. Diagram elements to include
   - Clear rectangular boxes for each component (CLI Core, Parser, Factory, Extractors, Request Layer, Downloader, Utils, External Tools).  
   - Arrows with labels for data flow (e.g., “URL → Parser”, “Stream descriptors → Downloader”).  
   - Color coding or shape variations:
     • Core system (blue)  
     • Plug-ins (green)  
     • External dependencies (orange)  
   - A legend explaining color/shape conventions.

7. Detailed capture of essential elements
   - Don’t just draw “Frontend” vs “Backend”—show the actual Go packages.  
   - Include the CI/CD box to reflect automated testing & release workflows.  
   - Show the global config package linking into Request Layer and Downloader.  
   - Capture the utilities as shared support services (pool, ffmpeg wrapper).  

By following these instructions and mapping the boxes & arrows to the actual Go packages and their interactions, you will produce a comprehensive, accurate architecture diagram for Lux that clearly shows its modular, extensible design, concurrent download engine, and CI/CD integration.
